It still looks fresh and is one of the best-known printed fabrics in the world.
artistBio: Maija Isola designed hundreds of prints for Marimekko. The company's founder, Armi Ratia, had said Marimekko would not print floral patterns. Isola answered with a set of flower designs, including Unikko, and Ratia accepted them. Unikko has been printed ever since in many colorways. Isola's work is in design museums, and she is honored as a leader of Finnish design.

title: Matyó Embroidery
medium: Embroidery on cotton, wool or silk
about: Matyó embroidery is covered in large, bright flowers: roses, peonies, tulips and buds, crowded together in red, pink, yellow, blue, green and black. Petals are often worked in satin stitch, so they shine. The flowers decorate aprons, shirt sleeves, cushions and household linens. Over time the designs grew denser and the colors brighter, until whole garments were covered.
artistBio: The Matyó are a Catholic community around Mezőkövesd in northeastern Hungary. Embroidery was done by women and was central to their festive dress. Patterns were often drawn by skilled 'pattern writers' and stitched by others. Matyó embroidery became a symbol of Hungarian folk art, and its folk art traditions are listed by UNESCO.

title: Blaudruck (Blueprint Cloth)
place: Germany, Austria, Czechia, Hungary and Slovakia
about: Blaudruck means 'blue print'. Printers press a sticky resist paste onto white cloth with carved wooden blocks. Then the cloth is dipped in an indigo vat again and again. When the paste is washed away, the printed areas stay white against deep blue. Patterns include small flowers, dots, leaves and stripes. The cloth was used for aprons, skirts, tablecloths and bedding.
artistBio: Blueprinting spread in Central Europe in the eighteenth century, as indigo became available, and most towns had a blue dyer. Factory printing later replaced most workshops. A few family workshops still carry on, some using blocks a century or more old. In 2018 UNESCO listed the craft as shared heritage of Austria, Czechia, Germany, Hungary and Slovakia.

title: St. Gallen Embroidery
artist: Embroiderers and manufacturers of St. Gallen
medium: Hand and machine embroidery on cotton and other fabrics
about: St. Gallen embroidery is fine white and colored work on cotton, often with cutwork and open areas that look like lace. It began as hand embroidery done at home in eastern Switzerland. In the nineteenth century, embroidery machines took over, first hand-operated, later the large Schiffli machines, which stitch with hundreds of needles at once. The patterns are delicate and very even.
artistBio: St. Gallen had been a linen-trading town since the Middle Ages. By the early twentieth century, its embroidery was among Switzerland's largest exports, and the city was a world center for it. The industry collapsed after the First World War but recovered in a smaller form. Today St. Gallen firms supply lace and embroidery to Paris fashion houses. The Textilmuseum St. Gallen holds its history.

title: Paisley Shawl
medium: Woven wool, silk or cotton, sometimes printed
about: Paisley shawls were large shawls covered in curving teardrop shapes called boteh, with wide patterned borders. They copied the costly hand-woven shawls of Kashmir, which were fashionable in Europe. Weavers in Paisley used drawlooms and later Jacquard looms to make them faster and cheaper. The teardrop shape became so linked with the town that it is still called the paisley pattern.
artistBio: Paisley was a busy weaving town near Glasgow. Its weavers were skilled and known for being well read and politically active. When fashion changed in the 1870s and shawls went out of style, the trade collapsed. Paisley Museum holds a large collection of shawls, pattern books and looms that tell the story.

title: Ayrshire Whitework
medium: White cotton embroidery with needle lace on fine muslin
about: Ayrshire work is white embroidery on very fine white muslin, done with tiny satin stitches and eyelets. Its special mark is the needle-lace fillings: small areas are cut away and filled with delicate lace stitches. It was used on christening gowns, baby caps, collars and cuffs. The best pieces are so fine that they look almost transparent.
artistBio: The style is credited to a Mrs. Jamieson of Ayr, who is said to have copied the lace fillings from a French christening robe. Thousands of women in Ayrshire and northern Ireland did the work at home for agents and merchants. It declined in the 1860s as machine embroidery spread and fashions changed. Many christening gowns survive as family heirlooms.

title: Carrickmacross Lace
medium: Appliqué of cambric or organdie on fine net
about: Carrickmacross lace is made by laying a fine cotton fabric over net, then outlining a design of flowers, leaves and scrolls with a thick thread couched down with tiny stitches. The extra fabric is cut away, leaving the solid shapes on the clear net. Small loops and filling stitches add texture. The finished lace is crisp and clean, with strong shapes.
artistBio: The craft is said to have begun in the 1820s when Mrs. Grey Porter taught local women a method she had seen in Italy. During the Great Famine, lace schools gave women a way to earn money. The St. Louis nuns of Carrickmacross later kept it going. The lace on the Duchess of Cambridge's 2011 wedding dress was made with the Carrickmacross method.

title: Termeh
about: Termeh is a fine woven cloth with small, dense patterns, especially the curved boteh (the paisley shape), set in rows on a deep red, green or black ground. It is woven with many colored weft threads, which the weaver selects for each part of the pattern. Termeh is used for covers and tablecloths, and was once worn as clothing.
artistBio: Termeh weaving was famed in Iran from at least Safavid times, with centers in Kerman and Yazd. Traditional termeh was woven on a drawloom, with an assistant above pulling the pattern cords. Only a few hand weavers remain today, mostly in Yazd, and most termeh is now made by machine. Iranian families often bring termeh out for Nowruz tables and weddings.

title: Afghan War Rugs
artist: Afghan weavers, including Baluch and Turkmen families
place: Afghanistan and refugee communities in Pakistan
about: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, weavers began knotting weapons into their rugs. Tanks, helicopters, rifles, grenades and fighter jets replace or sit among the old flower and medallion patterns. Some rugs include maps or words. From a distance, a rug may look traditional; up close, it is full of war. Later rugs also show events after 2001.
artistBio: War rugs were woven by families in Afghanistan and in refugee camps in Pakistan, often by women and children. Some recorded what weavers lived through; others were made because soldiers and foreign buyers wanted them. They raise hard questions about witness and commerce. Collectors and museums now keep them as a record of a long conflict seen by weavers.

title: Tiraz Textiles
artist: Weavers and embroiderers of state workshops (dar al-tiraz)
place: Egypt, Iraq, Yemen and other Islamic lands
medium: Linen or cotton with silk inscription bands
about: Tiraz are textiles with bands of writing woven or embroidered in silk across them. The inscriptions usually name the ruling caliph, give a blessing, and sometimes say where and when the cloth was made. The writing is in Arabic script, often in elegant Kufic letters. Many surviving pieces are fine linen from Egypt with a single band near the edge.
artistBio: Rulers ran special workshops called dar al-tiraz. Garments with tiraz bands were given as robes of honor to officials and guests, linking the wearer with the ruler. Many fragments survive from Egyptian burials, especially from the Fatimid period. Because they carry dates and names, they help scholars date other Islamic textiles.

title: Textiles from the Hallstatt Salt Mines
about: Deep in the salt mines of Hallstatt, miners left behind worn-out clothing, used as rags and lost in the tunnels. The salt preserved hundreds of wool fragments. They include fine twills, checks, stripes and narrow bands woven on tablets. Some still show their colors, blue, red, yellow and brown. Together they show how skilled and color-loving these early Europeans were.
artistBio: Hallstatt gave its name to a whole period of early Iron Age Europe. The textile finds have been studied for decades and have taught scholars a great deal about prehistoric spinning, weaving and dyeing. Many fragments are kept at the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Weavers have made reconstructions of the bands and cloths.

title: The Diligent Mother
about: A mother sits in a quiet room with her sewing things around her. Her young daughter stands beside her and shows her a piece of needlework, and the mother points to something in it, perhaps a mistake. A dog rests on the floor. Nothing dramatic happens. Chardin paints soft light, worn furniture and the calm work of teaching a child to sew.
artistBio: Chardin was a French painter known for still lifes and small scenes of everyday home life. He showed this picture at the Paris Salon of 1740, with its companion, Saying Grace, and both were presented to King Louis XV. The painting is now in the Louvre. Prints after it made the image widely known in the eighteenth century.

title: Weaver's Workshop
about: Decker painted the inside of a weaver's cottage again and again. A big wooden loom fills the dim room, and the weaver sits at it working the treadles and beater. Light comes through a small window. Often a woman or child sits nearby winding bobbins, with baskets and tools scattered about. The pictures show weaving as everyday family work at home.
artistBio: Cornelis Decker worked in Haarlem, a center of Dutch linen weaving and bleaching. He is best known for landscapes with cottages and for these weaver interiors, which survive in several versions in Dutch and other European museums. Few painters of his time took such interest in the working loom, so his pictures are valued by textile historians as well as art lovers.

title: The Dressmaking Studio
about: Women bend over their sewing in a small, crowded room. The patterns of their dresses, the cloth on the table and the wallpaper all blend together, so the figures seem to melt into the space. Faces are barely shown. Vuillard paints the soft hum of a working room, where fabric is everywhere and hands are always busy.
artistBio: Vuillard grew up among cloth and seamstresses. His mother ran a small corset-making and dressmaking workshop in the family apartment in Paris, and he painted it many times. He was a member of the Nabis, a group of young painters who loved flat patterns and decorative surfaces. Several versions of the dressmakers theme are in museums and private collections.

title: The Seamstress
about: A woman in a dark dress sits in profile on a chair, her body still and her work in her lap. The background is plain and the colors are muted greys and browns. Everything unneeded has been taken away. The painting is simple and quiet, and gives the seamstress a calm dignity, as if she were a figure in a much older painting.
artistBio: Helene Schjerfbeck is one of Finland's most admired painters. After years of travel, she lived quietly with her mother in the small town of Hyvinkää, where she painted local women, often working women, in a pared-down style. The Seamstress, also called The Working Woman, is in the Ateneum Art Museum in Helsinki.

title: The Spinner
about: A young barefoot woman stands in a sunny landscape, holding a distaff loaded with fiber in one hand. With the other she draws out the thread to the hanging spindle. She looks straight at us. The picture is polished and sweet, but it shows real hand spinning: the fiber on the distaff, the twist running down, the spindle turning.
artistBio: Bouguereau was one of the most successful French academic painters of the nineteenth century, famous for smooth finish and idealized figures. He painted many young women from Italian and French countryside life, often with spinning or other handwork. His reputation fell in the twentieth century, but his skill is again widely admired today.

title: Blackwork
medium: Black silk embroidery on white linen
about: Blackwork is embroidery in black thread on white or pale linen. Most of it is counted: the stitcher follows the threads of the cloth to make small, repeating geometric patterns that fill shapes like lace. The main stitch is double running, also called Holbein stitch, which goes along a line and back, filling the gaps. Done well, it looks the same on both sides.
artistBio: Blackwork was very fashionable in Tudor England, on shirts, collars, cuffs and caps. It is often linked with Catherine of Aragon and Spain, and was sometimes called Spanish work. Holbein's portraits show it on clothing in fine detail, which is why one stitch is named after him. Today embroiderers use blackwork for samplers, pictures and modern geometric designs.

title: Stumpwork (Raised Embroidery)
about: Stumpwork is embroidery that stands up from the surface. Shapes are padded with felt or wool, or built over carved wood. Petals, wings and leaves are worked in detached buttonhole stitch, sometimes over wire, so they can lift free of the ground. Beads, seed pearls, metal threads and tiny pieces of mica add sparkle. The result is a small, three-dimensional world.
artistBio: Raised work was popular in England between about 1650 and 1690. Girls often made it as a final test of their skill, after samplers, covering boxes, caskets and mirror frames with scenes from the Bible, kings and queens, gardens and animals. The name stumpwork came later, in the nineteenth century. Embroiderers today still use the methods for flowers and insects.

title: Soumak
about: Soumak is a way of wrapping weft yarn around warp threads instead of simply passing it over and under. A common form goes forward over four warps and back under two, again and again. This makes a strong, slightly raised surface with a fine braided look. Plain wefts are usually woven between soumak rows to hold it firm. The back is left with loose yarn ends.
artistBio: Weft wrapping is old and found in many places. The name soumak is often linked with Shemakha, a town in Azerbaijan, and Caucasian soumak rugs are especially famous. Weavers in Iran, Anatolia and Central Asia use it for rugs, bags and animal trappings. Modern tapestry and rug weavers use it to add texture and outline shapes.

title: Smocking
about: In smocking, fabric is gathered into many tiny, even pleats. Then the stitcher embroiders across the tops of the pleats with stitches such as cable, stem and honeycomb, holding them in patterns. The gathered fabric stays stretchy, so it can fit closely and still move. The stitches form bands of zigzags, diamonds and waves across a chest, cuffs or waist.
artistBio: English farmworkers in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries wore smock frocks: loose linen overgarments with smocked panels. Some say the patterns showed a worker's region or trade, though this is not certain. Later, smocking moved into fashion, especially for children's dresses, and became a favorite home sewing skill. It is still widely used today.

title: Ply-Split Braiding
place: Rajasthan and Gujarat, India, and elsewhere
medium: Twisted cords split by other cords
about: In ply-split braiding, the maker works with firm, plied cords. One cord is pushed through another, splitting it between its plies, using a hooked tool called a gripfid. By choosing which cords split which, the maker builds patterns and structures. The result is very strong and can be flat, tubular or sculptural. Two colors of cord make bold graphic designs.
artistBio: Herders in Rajasthan and Gujarat have long used the method to make camel girths and other gear, with striking patterns. The English weaver Peter Collingwood studied these girths and wrote about the method, bringing it to weavers in Europe and America. Today fiber artists use ply-split braiding for baskets, sculpture and jewelry.

title: Inkle Weaving
medium: Warp-faced bands on an inkle loom
about: Inkle weaving makes narrow, strong bands. On an inkle loom, warp threads are wound around pegs in a loop. Every other thread passes through a fixed string heddle; the rest are free. Lifting or pushing down the free threads opens the shed. Since the warp covers the weft completely, the pattern comes from how the colored warps are arranged: stripes, checks and small motifs.
artistBio: 'Inkle' is an old English word for a narrow linen tape. Shakespeare mentions inkles among a peddler's wares. Bands like these were used for ties, straps and trims. The simple table inkle loom became popular with hand weavers in the twentieth century and is still a favorite beginner's loom, used for belts, guitar straps and lanyards.

title: Otti Berger
place: Zmajevac (now Croatia); Dessau and Berlin, Germany
about: Otti Berger was born in a village that is now in Croatia and studied art in Zagreb. She lost much of her hearing as a child. In 1927 she came to the Bauhaus and joined the weaving workshop, where she soon stood out. She felt fabric with her hands and thought about cloth through touch. Later she ran her own studio in Berlin.
artistBio: Berger designed fabrics for industry, studying structure, sound absorption and feel, and she patented some of her designs. As a Jewish woman she was barred from working under the Nazis. She went to London but returned to Yugoslavia to care for her mother. In 1944 she was deported to Auschwitz and murdered. Her fabrics and samples are kept in Bauhaus collections.

title: Jack Lenor Larsen
about: Jack Lenor Larsen grew up in the Pacific Northwest and studied architecture and weaving before turning fully to cloth. He studied at Cranbrook Academy of Art, then moved to New York. In 1952 he started his own company. One of his first big jobs was the casement fabric for Lever House, a new glass office tower. He loved travel and handwork from around the world.
artistBio: Larsen's company made fabrics with the texture and life of handweaving, produced on power looms, and brought in methods from many cultures. He also wrote books, including one with Mildred Constantine that helped define fiber as art. His home and gardens in East Hampton, New York, became LongHouse Reserve, open to the public.

title: Claire Zeisler
about: Claire Zeisler was born in Cincinnati and lived most of her life in Chicago. She came to fiber art in middle age, after studying weaving and other arts. She soon left the flat loom behind and began making free-standing sculptures, tying, knotting and wrapping by hand. She was also a serious collector of art, which shaped her eye.
artistBio: Zeisler's best-known works are tall forms of knotted jute or wool, with masses of loose fiber spilling down onto the floor like hair or water. Bright reds were among her favorite colors. She was a leading figure in the fiber art movement of the 1960s and 1970s, and the Whitney Museum gave her a retrospective in 1979.

title: Yvonne Koolmatrie
about: Yvonne Koolmatrie is a Ngarrindjeri weaver from the lower Murray River region of South Australia. In the early 1980s she took a weaving workshop with the elder Dorothy Kartinyeri, one of the few people still keeping the old method alive. Koolmatrie decided to carry it on. She gathers river sedge, prepares it, and coils it with great patience.
artistBio: Koolmatrie makes traditional forms such as fish and eel traps and baskets, and also sculptures of animals, boats and even aircraft. Her work keeps Ngarrindjeri weaving alive and teaches it to others. In 1997 she represented Australia at the Venice Biennale with Emily Kame Kngwarreye and Judy Watson. Her work is in major Australian museums.

title: Lucienne Day
about: Lucienne Day studied printed textiles at the Royal College of Art in London. She married the furniture designer Robin Day, and the two became one of the best-known design couples of postwar Britain. Her breakthrough came in 1951 with Calyx, a furnishing fabric of spindly lines and cup-shaped flowers, made for the Festival of Britain and sold by Heal's.
artistBio: Calyx won prizes and changed British taste, moving it away from old-fashioned floral chintz toward abstract modern patterns inspired by art and plants. Day designed many fabrics, as well as wallpapers, carpets and ceramics. Later she made 'silk mosaics', wall hangings pieced from small squares of silk. Her work is in the V&A and other museums.

title: The Flax Fibers of Dzudzuana Cave
about: In 2009, scientists reported finding tiny flax fibers in layers of Dzudzuana Cave in the Caucasus mountains of Georgia, about 30,000 years old. Under the microscope, some fibers were twisted, which suggests they had been made into cord or thread. Some appeared to have been colored. The flax was wild; farming had not yet begun.
artistBio: Fibers rot easily, so evidence of very early textiles is rare. These finds suggest that Ice Age people were already twisting plant fiber into string, perhaps for sewing, tying, baskets or simple cloth. Some scholars debate how to read the evidence. Still, the find pushes the story of thread back far beyond the beginnings of weaving and farming.

title: The Lowell Mill Girls
about: Lowell was built as a planned mill town, where water power ran large cotton mills. The owners hired young women from New England farms to run the spinning and weaving machines. They lived in company boarding houses under strict rules and worked long days. Many sent money home or saved for school or marriage. Some wrote for a magazine, the Lowell Offering.
artistBio: When the companies cut wages and raised rents, the women walked out in 1834 and 1836. In the 1840s, led by people such as Sarah Bagley, they petitioned for a ten-hour working day. They were among the first American industrial workers to organize. Later, immigrant workers replaced them in the mills. Their story is told at Lowell National Historical Park.

title: Turkey Red
about: Turkey red is a bright, very fast red on cotton, made with madder. Cotton does not take madder easily, so the process was long: the cloth was treated again and again with oil, alkali, alum and other materials, then dyed and finished. It could take weeks and many stages. The result was a strong, clear red that did not fade in washing or sun.
artistBio: The method came from India and the eastern Mediterranean, and Europeans called it Turkey red. In the eighteenth century, dyers brought it to France and Britain. The Vale of Leven in Scotland became famous for Turkey red cloth, printed with patterns and sold worldwide. After synthetic alizarin was made in 1869, the old madder method slowly ended.

title: Logwood
place: Yucatán, Central America and the Caribbean
medium: Purple, blue and black dye from heartwood
about: Logwood dye comes from the dark red heartwood of a small tree that grows around the Bay of Campeche and in Central America. The wood is chipped and soaked to release its color. Depending on the mordant, it gives purples, greys and blues, and with iron it makes deep, rich blacks. It was one of the most important black dyes for wool, silk and cotton.
artistBio: Spanish ships brought logwood to Europe in the sixteenth century. Early dyes made with it faded, and in Elizabethan England its use was banned for a time; the ban was lifted in the seventeenth century as dyers learned to fix it. Logwood cutting shaped the history of Belize, with hard labor by enslaved Africans. A form of the dye is still used to stain cells in laboratories.

title: The Spinning Jenny
about: The spinning jenny let one person spin several threads at once. A single large wheel, turned by hand, drove a row of spindles. Fiber was held in a sliding carriage that the spinner drew back to stretch the threads, then pushed forward as the yarn wound on. The first jennies had eight spindles; later ones had many more. The yarn was soft, best for weft.
artistBio: James Hargreaves, a weaver in Lancashire, built the jenny in the 1760s and patented it in 1770. Hand spinners feared losing work, and some jennies were smashed. Still, it spread fast in cottages and small workshops. It was soon joined by Arkwright's water frame and then Crompton's mule, which moved spinning into factories.

title: The Charkha
about: The charkha is an Indian spinning wheel, used mostly for cotton. The spinner turns the wheel with one hand, which spins a small spindle at high speed, while the other hand draws out the cotton fiber from a roll. Some charkhas are large and stand on the floor. The box charkha folds into a case and can be carried like a book.
artistBio: Spinning wheels were used in India for centuries. In the 1920s, Mahatma Gandhi made the charkha a symbol of the freedom movement. He asked Indians to spin their own yarn and wear handwoven khadi instead of imported mill cloth. The charkha appeared on the Indian National Congress flag. In the national flag adopted in 1947, it was replaced by the Ashoka wheel.
